title: Doctors May Ignore Your Messages If They’re Not Well-Written - Nautilus
gist: A JAMA Network Open study finds that how patients write messages in doctor portals can determine whether they get a reply at all, because a human triage layer of nurses and medical assistants—subject to bias and error—decides which messages reach the physician.

insights.claim: A JAMA Network Open study finds the way patients write messages to doctors through patient portals can determine whether they get a reply at all.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Implies message phrasing is an actionable variable affecting patients' access to care.
insights.locator: finds that the way we write messages to doctors can determine whether or not we get a reply

insights.claim: Portal messages usually pass through a human layer of nurses, medical assistants, and other healthcare workers who decide whether to escalate a message to the physician, triaging them like emergency-room patients.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Reveals the hidden gatekeeping step that shapes whether patient concerns reach a doctor.
insights.locator: there’s a human layer between you and your physician

insights.claim: Because human staff triage the messages, escalation is subject to human error, inherent biases, and other issues.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Flags equity and quality-of-care risks in portal-based communication systems.
insights.locator: where there are humans, there’s human error, inherent biases
